passage: My friend Binita and I have joked about everything since Class 8. She calls me Mr Sleepy, I call her Wrong Turn because she gets lost in her own house. It's ours, and I love it. Last week in the canteen I posted a meme of her mixing up two buses and put it in the class chat. Twenty people reacted with 😂. Binita typed "haha" and nothing else. In person she was quiet and kept looking at her tray. I went cold, because she always sends me ten emojis back. I said sorry that evening. She told me she liked being teased by me, but not with an audience. I've learnt to watch her face, not just the reactions. - Tenzin

qa.q: Where did Tenzin post the meme about Binita?
qa.a: He put it in the class chat.

qa.q: What did Binita's short 'haha' and quiet mood suggest?
qa.a: Most likely she was hurt or embarrassed by the audience, since she usually sends many emojis; another possibility is that she was just tired.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do to keep the banter fun for both of them?
qa.a: Keep the jokes private, check Binita's response each time, and stop as soon as she seems uncomfortable.

qa.q: How might the twenty classmates' laughing reactions have felt to Binita?
qa.a: It may have felt like being laughed at by a crowd instead of joking with a close friend, even if each classmate meant no harm.

grounding: Banter signals closeness, but teasing hurts when one person isn't enjoying it; watching the response is the guide.

passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. During the group task I overheard Madhav calling Shankar "Professor Snail" because he takes time on his answers. The other boys laughed, and Madhav grinned at Shankar as he'd do with a friend. Shankar smiled thinly, then stopped writing and moved his chair a little away. He hadn't said anything, but he didn't contribute again that period. The two sit together at lunch, so I suspect Madhav means no harm, and I can't be sure how Shankar felt. I asked Shankar quietly afterwards whether he was fine with the nickname. He said he wasn't sure. Next I'll talk with Madhav about watching the other person's reaction, and check in with Shankar again.

qa.q: What nickname did Madhav use for Shankar?
qa.a: Madhav called him Professor Snail because he takes time on his answers.

qa.q: What did Shankar's thin smile and moving away suggest?
qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable, and possibly hurt, though the teacher can't be sure; another reading is that he was simply concentrating.

qa.q: What could the teacher say to Madhav?
qa.a: Explain that banter works when both people enjoy it, and that Shankar's reaction is the guide to when it should stop.

qa.q: How might Madhav see the nickname differently from Shankar?
qa.a: Madhav probably thinks it is friendly play like their usual jokes at lunch, while Shankar may feel laughed at in front of the other boys.

grounding: Banter and nicknames signal closeness but hurt when one person doesn't enjoy the teasing; the reaction guides when to stop.

passage:
Tuesday
Ira has this laugh that sounds like a squeaky gate. It's honestly the best laugh in the world. So I've started doing an impression of it whenever she laughs. Everyone cracks up.
The first few times she laughed too and swatted me.
Today in the canteen I did it again, and she didn't laugh. She put her hand over her mouth and went quiet for the rest of lunch. Later in class, when something was funny, she just smiled with her lips closed.
That's when I got it. She was trying not to laugh because of me.
After school I said, "Ira, the gate thing. Is it bothering you?"
She said, "A bit. Now I'm scared to laugh."
I felt awful. I told her I love her laugh, which is true, and that I'm done with the impression.
She laughed properly at the bus stop. Squeaky gate. Perfect.
- Kiran

qa.q: What does Ira's laugh sound like?
qa.a: It sounds like a squeaky gate.

qa.q: What does Ira's hand over her mouth suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed and self-conscious, no longer enjoying the teasing and scared to laugh.

qa.q: How did Kiran know when to stop, and what did Kiran do?
qa.a: Kiran noticed Ira's changed response, asked directly, apologised, and stopped the impression.

qa.q: What was it like for Ira when the teasing kept going?
qa.a: It went from playful to hurtful, making Ira hide something about herself that she used to enjoy.

grounding: The diary shows playful teasing turning hurtful when the other person stops enjoying it, and the teaser noticing and stopping.

passage:
At the tea stall by the bus stand in Ravangla, Pema and Darshan were the kings of jokes. He teased her about her bicycle that squeaked like a goat; she teased him about his hair that looked like a bird's nest. The tea-shop owner laughed along every morning.
On Monday Darshan tried a new one. "Pema, smile! Oh wait, show us the gap!" Pema had lost a front tooth in a fall last month.
A few people laughed. Pema smiled with closed lips and looked down into her tea.
Darshan waited for her comeback. It didn't come.
He noticed she had pulled her scarf up a little over her mouth.
"Hey," he said, quieter. "That one wasn't funny, was it?"
She shook her head.
"Sorry. Goat bicycle only from now."
Pema let out a breath. "Bird's nest," she said, and they both laughed.

qa.q: What did Pema's bicycle squeak like?
qa.a: It squeaked like a goat.

qa.q: What did Pema's closed-lip smile and pulled-up scarf suggest?
qa.a: They suggested she felt embarrassed and hurt about her missing tooth, not enjoying the joke.

qa.q: How did Darshan know when the joke should stop?
qa.a: He noticed her comeback didn't come and she covered her mouth, so he asked and apologised.

qa.q: How might the people who laughed have seen the tooth joke?
qa.a: They probably saw it as part of the usual morning banter, not noticing Pema's discomfort.

grounding: The scene shows playful teasing signalling closeness until one joke hurts, and watching the other's response to know when to stop.

passage: In their Mexico City school, Diego had called Yosef "Profesor" since the first week, because of the round glasses and the way Yosef explained football tactics with salt shakers. Yosef usually bowed and answered in a fake lecture voice, and the table cracked up. On Thursday the maths tests came back. Yosef's had a big red 5 on it, and he slid it into his bag fast. At lunch Diego, who hadn't noticed, called across the table, "Profesor! Explain to us the secrets of algebra!" A few people laughed. Yosef didn't bow. He smiled, but only with his mouth, and went back to his sandwich. Diego waited for the lecture voice. It didn't come. He looked at Yosef's bag, then at his face, and let it drop. "Actually, forget algebra. Explain why our team lost on Sunday." Yosef let out a breath and picked up a salt shaker. After school Diego asked, "The nickname. Still okay?" "Mostly," Yosef said. "Not today."

qa.q: What mark was on Yosef's maths test?
qa.a: It had a big red 5 on it.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when he smiled only with his mouth?
qa.a: Yosef was likely embarrassed and low after the bad test, so the nickname stung that day; it might also have been simple tiredness, which is why checking later mattered.

qa.q: What did Diego notice, and what did he do?
qa.a: Diego noticed the missing lecture voice and the tight smile, switched the topic to the match, and later asked whether the nickname was still okay. 👍

qa.q: What would have changed if Diego had kept pushing the joke?
qa.a: Yosef would likely have felt mocked about the grade in front of everyone, and the nickname could have turned from closeness into hurt.

grounding: It shows a nickname and banter signalling closeness, and a teenager reading the other boy's response to know when play should stop.
